paragraphs: On the day news of Huan Xuan’s death reached Jiankang, the palace steps were being scrubbed. The Jin banners hastily raised several months earlier had grown shabby in the river rain, and the stitching on one corner had split another inch. A palace attendant in charge of the old flags took the victory dispatch and ran halfway down the gallery, only to stop and ask when the Jin emperor would return. The young maid beside him did not know either. She set down the mud-stained cloth in her hand and went to fetch water for the messenger.

Military families arriving from Jingkou searched for old service registers outside the granary. Many recognized their unit numbers from the days of Xie Xuan but not the newly named government offices. The officials in charge still made them stand in line. At the back, an old woman afraid that her son’s name would be overlooked clutched a wooden name plaque polished bright by handling and waited all morning. In the afternoon, the office was suddenly called upon to prepare the restoration ceremony, and every scribe was taken away to copy edicts. The woman refused to leave. A gate soldier had no choice but to lend her a stool and ask her to come back the next day.

Liu Yu sent men along the river to welcome the imperial party. When the Jin emperor escaped from Huan’s troops, hardly any attendants remained with him, and he was repeatedly frightened on the journey back to Jiankang. By the time the procession and edicts for his restoration were ready, spring had come in another year. The Jin flags the Beifu Army had raised when it took the city were taken down and replaced with twelve ceremonial banners patched together from the old palace stores. Court ritualists argued endlessly over the hymns, the carriages, and the wording of the proclamations.

The imperial workshop lacked jade, so an old ornament was used to replace one of the beads hanging from the crown. The military dispatches from the time Fu Jian had advanced to the Fei River lay buried beneath these memorials, only to be brought out now and again by someone reminding the restored court that a stronger rival state still stood on the northern bank.

On the day of the ceremony Sima Dezong sat on the throne with his head tilted toward the attendant quietly prompting him. As the imperial seal came down on the edict, a censor steadied his hand. The red impression fell slightly askew. Acclamations filled the hall once more. Liu Yu bowed behind the assembled officials. Seeing the blue veins standing out on the emperor’s thin wrist, he suddenly remembered Fu Jian personally turning the pages of the grain and troop registers beside the Fei. The two emperors were separated by a thousand li and by decades of history, yet both had power over the people waiting for grain before Liu Yu’s eyes.

The restoration ceremony was not yet over when petitioners began waiting before the Secretariat. The first matter presented was not a register of pensions for the war dead, but a deed to an old estate in Danyang. A former Wang-family official arrived with the clan’s scribes, claiming that Huan Xuan had unlawfully confiscated land granted by a former emperor. Now that the Jin dynasty had been restored, it ought to be returned without delay.

The deed recorded three thousand one hundred mu, its ink of varying shades, and included a copy of an imperial grant from decades earlier. Liu Muzhi spread the recent household registers beside it. Two hundred and seventy-three families still lived on the land. Some were old estate tenants; others had taken refuge there during Sun En’s uprising. In more than forty households the men had followed the Beifu Army against Huan Xuan; only yesterday had their wives received news that their husbands were dead.

An officer at the hearing struck the table first. The refugees had harvested grain from those fields for two seasons, he said; after helping restore Jin, why should they pay rent to aristocrats again? The Wang-family retainer’s face darkened. “The estate is ancestral property, sealed by the court. If today the state treats a soldier’s seizure as a valid deed, who will obey an imperial command tomorrow?”

Liu Yu did not reply. He summoned the county clerk responsible for household registration. The clerk explained that the spring floods had broken the old drainage channel west of the estate. More than twenty families were still living in sheds. If the households were evicted immediately, the county could not even find enough vacant land to resettle them. The Wang retainer said the commandery government could find them other quarters. Liu Yu asked whether the commandery had empty fields, how long the move would take, and who would reimburse the seed sown in the first half of the season. The retainer shook his deed and said the court must surely settle such questions.
An old soldier stood below the steps, blood still crusted on his clothes. “Your land is written down plainly enough,” he said. “The clerks have not even learned all the names of our dead.”

Liu Yu placed both sets of papers on the table, weighing each down with a paperweight. “Nothing moves for now,” he said. “Those farming the land will continue to farm it. No soldier may allot himself disputed fields, and no former owner may reclaim them by force. Rent grain is to be sealed in the county granary under a separate account. Anyone who wishes to bring a claim must produce the old deeds and new evidence. We will examine household by household who drove whom away in the first place.”

Neither side was satisfied. The Wang representative said the court had lost its legitimacy; the officer said the Beifu soldiers had fought only to guard fields for their former owners. Liu Yu told the Secretariat to record both sets of claims precisely and affixed the public seal beneath the order. As he escorted the Wang retainer out, the old man suddenly asked, “General, when you broke into Jiankang, if we had not opened the gates, would you still be examining these cases household by household?”
Liu Yu looked at him for a moment. “I have entered the city. You may make your record of what happened before. The people on that estate must not be made to die for it all over again this year.”

That evening Liu Muzhi brought several volumes of cases still awaiting inventory: land Huan Xuan had seized, land temporarily distributed by Chu troops, land appropriated by meritorious Beifu officers, and fields reclaimed by families returning after flight. Often all four kinds lay on a single map. In the Qin camp Liu Yu had seen guest-register clerks lay out competing old documents for witnesses to examine. But Chang’an had years of reconciled accounts and steady grain transport; in the south, county clerks had served three masters in succession, and many had not even recovered their official seals. Liu Muzhi said it could take more than a year to examine every household with men like these. Liu Yu asked whether they might begin with a few counties. They debated the matter until the third night-watch drum, finally marking three counties near Jingkou on the map.

A dozen or so days later Liu Yu returned to Jingkou. Hearing he had come, many soldiers' wives and dependents gathered before the county office before dawn. Most did not ask about honors or titles. They asked whether their husbands' remains could be found, whether last season’s pay could still be collected, and whether children without land could be entered in the registers of military households.

A young woman cradling a cracked iron helmet reached the front of the line only after the sun was high and gave the clerk her husband’s name. Sun Huaide had been killed in the pursuit near Fuzhou Mountain. His name appeared in an old military register, but the commander’s validating seal was missing; that commander had also died in battle. By established procedure, the county clerk told her to obtain the seal. The woman asked which grave she ought to visit to request it. Around her, people silently averted their eyes.

Liu Yu took the helmet. A cut from a blade still marked its rim, and the characters engraved inside had been eaten away by sweat. The clerk said two men from Sun Huaide’s squad were alive and could identify the helmet, but the old rules accepted only the commander’s signature and seal. Liu Yu summoned both men, found another casualty register, and laid the three kinds of evidence together. One comrade remembered lending Sun Huaide half a waterskin shortly before he died; the other said Sun had asked him to bring his monthly pay home to his wife and children. Liu Yu listened and ordered the first allotment of emergency grain issued to the woman. The missing commander seal would be addressed later through review and supplementary evidence at the army office.

From that day on, the three counties around Jingkou no longer treated a commander’s single seal as the sole proof of a death in service. Testimony from two comrades, marks on personal effects, burial lists, and casualty registers could corroborate one another. When testimony conflicted, the case was marked for further examination, but limited emergency grain was issued first, so that a family would not starve while waiting for a verdict.

Military clerks complained that the procedure was cumbersome. Liu Muzhi said the old method had relied on a single seal; when that seal was missing, there was not even anyone left to provide another. With three more forms of evidence, at least one was likely to survive in the world. Liu Yu did not praise him. He simply ordered the county office to preserve all the evidence as originally given, so that if anyone later alleged fraud, investigators could trace precisely who had testified.

The first several hundred households received deeds to fields or relief grain for their losses. In the second month, relatives began quarreling over the division of land, and some officers secretly entered men from their personal retinues on the rolls of the fallen. Liu Yu ordered a fresh check against the military registers. An old commander was found to have taken money and silk from a powerful family in exchange for arranging false land awards. The man had served in the Jingkou uprising and presumed upon his record. With several soldiers he assaulted the officials measuring the fields.

Brought under guard to the army office, he shouted that when Liu Yu first raised the military banner, not one of them had escaped shedding blood. Liu Yu ordered the land seizure and the assault on officials tried as separate charges, with witnesses heard in turn. Under the military regulations the offenses merited execution, and he was put to death at the camp gate the following day. His genuine service in battle was entered separately, and the military allowance paid to his aged mother was not reduced because of his crime.

Resentment spread through the army. Some said their commander now trusted civilian clerks too much. Others retold the old officer’s cries at his execution as proof that Liu Yu had cast aside his comrades. Days later Jingkou’s military granary reported its stocks, and the emergency grain set aside was indeed insufficient. Liu Muzhi had to pursue arrears county by county. Then new petitioners came: the fields recently allotted to military households were low-lying and salty. Possession of a title deed did not mean they could harvest even half a dou of millet.

At the edge of one field Sun Huaide’s wife showed Liu Yu where rainwater pooled over the shallow plots. The ditch at the southern end had been blocked by the wall of an old estate. She had eaten all her emergency grain, and when her child had developed a fever a few days earlier she had had no money even for medicine. Liu Yu climbed down into the ditch and sank more than an inch into the mud. Only then did he realize that the county surveyor’s map recorded the acreage but not the flow of water. Back at the county office he ordered the surveyors to inspect the old channel and neighboring fields together. If another ditch had to be dug, the adjoining households must first be heard; a new deed must not set off yet another fight over water.

The woman watched him pull off his wet boots. She did not thank him for his benevolence. She asked only whether the channel could be repaired before the following spring. Liu Yu said that depended on labor and the county’s grain reserves. She nodded and returned the broken helmet to her basket. More than the imperial seal that had fallen askew in the great palace hall, she wanted to know whether next year’s rice shoots would drown.

The methods used in the three counties gradually spread to Jinling and Danyang. Some places were willing to follow them; elsewhere even the basic military registers had been lost. Some magistrates exploited the new rules to take payments from both sides, preserving the best land for great families and allotting barren ground to military households.

Gradually Liu Yu came to see that tens of thousands of soldiers could march beneath a single banner, while the clerks of hundreds of counties each answered to a different patron. He could dismiss a few corrupt officials, and the court could issue edicts demanding accountability. But someone still had to measure the fields, and someone still had to escort the grain. An empty granary would not be full the following morning merely because nobles and generals had made their peace that day.

Several months after the restoration, the petitioners' drum sounded again outside the palace gate. Sun Huaide’s wife arrived with eleven military widows and dependents from Guangling. The official receiving their petitions explained that the Jingkou procedure was still experimental; Guangling must wait for the military office to verify its rolls. The woman asked whether men killed in different places were buried in different earth and therefore deserved different grain.

The petition officer could find no answer. He sealed their papers and sent them to the Secretariat. By the time Liu Yu saw the petitions, their edges bore finger marks left by sweat. He ordered a temporary allotment of relief and asked Liu Muzhi for the actual figures on Guangling’s officials and granaries. Merely saying “follow the Jingkou precedent” would not do.

Just then a state letter arrived from north of the Yangtze. After the chaos under Huan Xuan, three market towns south of the Fei had received Qin protection for their grain deliveries. Several groups of refugees had taken out temporary guest registrations or Qin household registrations there, and some garrison troops were being paid against Qin grain vouchers. Now that the Jin dynasty had been restored, the former local officials demanded the return of the towns and an end to alterations in household registration. But the Qin troops replied that the people had invited them to begin with, that their expenditures on food and defenses were documented, and that one Jin edict proclaiming a restoration could not simply require them to abandon the towns.

When members of the Jin imperial clan heard this, they called for an immediate campaign against the three towns. Some argued that border families who had accepted Qin registration were traitors and must be forcibly moved back. Others proposed allowing the towns to choose their own allegiance; why begin another war over a few small places? Liu Yu separated the records of their granaries and fields into several piles: official dispatches from before the towns changed hands; Qin vouchers for grain and medical aid; and petitions local families had submitted to both courts at once. In the same household, a husband wanted to keep his Jin registration, while his wife drew grain on Qin vouchers. When a child was born they could quarrel furiously over which reign title to enter for the year.

Liu Yu drafted a state letter demanding that Qin cease registering new households farther south and sending additional garrisons; the status of former Jin territory was to be investigated town by town. Those wishing to return south must not be stopped; those choosing to remain for the time being on the northern bank must not be dragged back by force. Some at court objected that these terms amounted to acknowledging Qin’s enticement of Jin subjects. Liu Yu asked who, when those towns had run out of grain, had actually delivered grain to them. The imperial relatives had no answer and turned instead to borders, legitimate calendars, and ancestors. Liu Yu included those concerns in the letter but insisted upon retaining the provision allowing the people themselves to state whether they wished to stay or leave.

Fu Jian’s reply came swiftly down from the Huai. The town boundaries could be surveyed, grain vouchers reconciled, and garrison arrangements redrawn. But civilians already entered in household registers could not be transferred by headcount like military equipment. Liu Yu read the letter and did not fold it for a long time. Fu Jian possessed twenty years' accumulation of military registers, roads, and granaries, and could afford to write his conditions with composure. Liu Yu had only just recovered Jiankang and still owed much that he had promised. Each man’s argument on paper had its own foundation, but the women and children of the three towns would not be spared tomorrow’s taxes simply because one side put its case more persuasively.

That night Liu Muzhi arrived with the grain accounts and pressed him: if Qin troops continued to hold the towns, would Beifu attack? Liu Yu spread the letter on the table. “First send men to examine the boundaries and the grain records. Qin must not move south; Jin must not attack without orders. Until the facts are established, neither garrison may seize supplies from civilian households to make up unpaid wages.”
“And if they refuse?”
“Then write down their refusal in their own words.”
There was no trace of a smile on Liu Muzhi’s face. “The day will come when we must draw our swords.”

Liu Yu gazed at a new canal plan from Jingkou. On it, the boundaries of three families' fields had been amended again and again in washed ink. “When that day comes, we will draw them,” he said. “For now, let us settle one more case.”

At the top of the case file lay a petition from a soldier’s wife whose husband had been missing for five years. She asked to have the old marriage entry struck from the register so she could marry someone else. The county office had not verified the death rolls; it would neither grant her a survivor’s allowance nor permit her registration to be changed. At the end of her petition she had written: “I cannot keep faith forever with a name whose bearer may be alive or dead, and let my two little sons starve beside me.”

The wind and rain outside the palace had not stopped. Northern soldiers were still thirty li away. Liu Yu told the clerks to hear this case first the following day and sent someone to investigate the last ferry where the missing soldier had served. Rain fell on Qin’s reply by the edge of the table, its ink not yet quite dry. The small petition from one family had already been turned so often that the edges were fraying.
The Jin banners had risen again over Jiankang. Beneath them, people still had to live, one day after another.
